sentences.text: Pachycheilosuchus is notable for having procoelous vertebrae, a feature otherwise found only in derived eusuchian crocodilians.
These vertebrae articulate with a concave anterior surface and a convex posterior surface.
The animal possessed a short and flat snout.
Its ulna, the major bone of the forearm, was strongly curved.
Pachycheilosuchus was not a large crocodylomorph, with the longest collected thigh bone measuring only 91.2 millimeters.
A 49 millimeter-long crocodyloid egg recovered with fossils suggests that some individuals were sexually mature at a length of 63.5 centimeters.
The genus Pachycheilosuchus was named and described by Jack Rogers in 2003.
Fossils of crocodylomorphs from Glen Rose were previously known under the informal designation "Glen Rose form".
These fossils included a skull at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History and two partial skeletons at the Texas Memorial Museum, along with isolated bones.
The skull and two skeletons lacked the "lip" jaw and procervical vertebrae, meaning they do not belong to Pachycheilosuchus but to an undescribed form.
However, some of the isolated bones do belong to Pachycheilosuchus.
With the description of Pachycheilosuchus, it appears that the "Glen Rose form" was a paleontological chimera.
A puncture mark measuring 5 millimeters by 6.5 millimeters on a maxilla was probably made by a larger predator.
Researchers suggest that Pachycheilosuchus likely evolved procoely independently because it lacked other eusuchian characteristics.
Pachycheilosuchus is classified within the family Hylaeochampsidae.
Pachycheilosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
Pachycheilosuchus lived in Texas, United States, during the Early Cretaceous period.
Pachycheilosuchus lived during the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether the previously known "Glen Rose Form" represents a single species or multiple forms, as some fossils lack the defining features of Pachycheilosuchus.
